subject: RStan vs. R's glm() function for logistic regression

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: RStan vs. R's glm() function for logistic regression
parts:
I was running some tests for speed, and thought people
might like to see the results. The bottom line is
that R's glm() function is about 60 times faster than
Stan at fitting a simple logistic regression.

Here's the table, where K is number of predictors,
and N is the number of dimensions.

The simulated data for predictors and coefficients
were both indepdent unit normal, which is probably
not the most realistic way to set up such a test.
We'll be running some more realistic tests and looking
at hierarchical models vs. R packages lme and blme.

Here's the results:

K N stan() glm()
time
---------------------------------------------------
10 1,000 1s 0s
10 10,000 7s 0s
10 100,000 1m 2s
10 1,000,000 10m 20s

20 1,000 1s 0s
20 10,000 20s 0s
20 100,000 2m 2s

40 1,000 3s 0s
40 10,000 40s 0s

80 1,000 6s 0s*
10,000 1m 1s*

160 1,000 20s 1s*
160 10,000 3m 3s

320 1,000 2m 2s*

640 1,000 9m 8s*

* = convergence issue for glm(), which isn't solved by lowering
step size or increasing the number of iterations; whether
glm() failed often depended on the parameters themselves

Stan will continue to scale, at about the same rate --- I
just got tired waiting for the results and was too lazy
to automate the test process.

Stan runs consist of 200 iterations on 4 chains, all split Rhat < 1.1,
and all parameters > 50 ESS.

glm() run with default settings:

glm_fit <- glm(y ~ x,family=binomial(link=logit))


Stan model, with prior for beta fixed to the true value:

data {
int<lower=1> K;
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
matrix[N,K] x;
}
parameters {
vector[K] beta;
}
model {
beta ~ normal(0,1);
y ~ bernoulli_logit(x * beta);
}

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RStan vs. R's glm() function for logistic regression
parts:
On 5/21/13 5:02 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Just out of curiosity, how fast do these compare to running stan in its mode-finding setting?

Good question. Unfortunately, the answer with the optimizer
currently plugged into RStan 1.3 is 2.3 minutes, which is roughly
the same amount of time as it takes Stan to run NUTS. Here's
the report:

Iteration 1. Log joint probability = -3216.52. Improved by 3714.96.
Iteration 2. Log joint probability = -2083.11. Improved by 1133.4.
Iteration 3. Log joint probability = -1488.77. Improved by 594.344.
Iteration 4. Log joint probability = -1187.62. Improved by 301.151.
Iteration 5. Log joint probability = -1066.97. Improved by 120.65.
Iteration 6. Log joint probability = -1040.77. Improved by 26.2012.
Iteration 7. Log joint probability = -1039.23. Improved by 1.53311.
Iteration 8. Log joint probability = -1039.23. Improved by 0.00638312.
Iteration 9. Log joint probability = -1039.23. Improved by 1.21573e-07.

The answers match pretty closely for glm(), Stan NUTS, Stan optimization,
and the simulated parameters.

Those last three iterations don't gain us much, especially the last two,
so we could perhaps shave 20% off the optimization time by imposing a less
stringent convergence criterion.

So the comparison for the test I just ran is this:

K N Stan NUTS glm() Stan optimize
160 10,000 3m 3s 2m


I should also point out that we have a lot of room for
improvement in Stan for these models through writing a custom
logistic_regression() distribution, which would look like.

y ~ logistic_regression(x,beta);

This will be several times faster than what we do now, but
is unlikely to be 60 times faster. It'll speed up both optimization
and sampling.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RStan vs. R's glm() function for logistic regression
parts:
I could e-mail the data, but it's 13MB gzipped.
(10K instances * 160 params = 1.6 million double values)

Or you can generate your own data using the following R code,
which is what I used for the simulations. Note that there's
an intercept term. (I also had a line setting beta[2] to -1 for
some reason, but I removed it.)


-------------logistic-sim.R-----------------------

library("rstan");

inv_logit <- function(u) {
return(1 / (1 + exp(-u)));
}

K <- 160;
N <- 10000;
sigma_beta <- 1;
beta <- rnorm(K,mean=0,sd=sigma_beta);
sigma_x <- 1;
x <- matrix(rnorm(N*K,mean=0,sd=sigma_x),nrow=N,ncol=K);
x[,1] <- rep(1,N);
y <- rep(NA,N);
for (n in 1:N) {
y[n] <- rbinom(1,1,inv_logit(x[n,] %*% beta));
}

fit <- stan("logistic.stan", data=c("K","N","y","x"), chains=1, iter=2, init=0);

start_time_stanopt <- Sys.time()
ofit <- optimizing(get_stanmodel(fit), data=list(K=K,N=N,y=y,x=x), init=0);
end_time_stanopt <- Sys.time();
elapsed_time_stanopt <- end_time_stanopt - start_time_stanopt;

start_time_glm <- Sys.time()
glm_fit <- glm(y ~ x,family=binomial(link=logit))

end_time_glm <- Sys.time();
elapsed_time_glm <- end_time_glm - start_time_glm;

start_time <- Sys.time()
fit <- stan("logistic.stan", data=c("K","N","y","x"), chains=4, iter=200, init=0, fit=fit);
end_time <- Sys.time();
elapsed_time <- end_time - start_time;
print("");
print("elapsed time, stan():"); print(elapsed_time);
print("elapsed time, glm():"); print(elapsed_time_glm);

---------------------------------------------------------------------

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RStan vs. R's glm() function for logistic regression
parts:
Was that using Newton's method or BFGS? The convergence speed (in
iterations) looks more like Newton (a.k.a. iteratively reweighted
least squares). That Newton implementation is getting the Hessian in a
pretty naive way, which for LR can be much more heavily optimized.

Are we linking against a BLAS? I've been meaning to bring that up as a
possible area for optimization. I would assume that glm is using some
kind of optimized BLAS, which makes a big, big difference when your
primary computational operation is matrix multiplication and
inversion.

Matt

Ok, I just did a quick test of BFGS using the model and data generation scripts Bob sent.  This is with K = 160 and N = 10,000

Marcus-Brubakers-MacBook-Pro:stan mbrubake$ time ./logistic --data=logisitic.data --point_estimate_bfgs --init=0 --refresh=5

user 0m12.912s

So, in short, 13s.  Now, a few caveats:

1) The BFGS implementation is currently bad at detecting convergence.  If it was better at this, that would probably be 10s.
2) Somewhere around 7 or 8 seconds is spent before the first iteration is ever run.  I suspect that most of this is caused by reading in the data from the R dump format.
3) This timing is on a different machine than Bob's, but I suspect my 3-4yr old macbook pro is probably slower than whatever Bob was running on.

If we assumed that 1&2 could be resolved, the time would be more like 3 or 4 seconds which is basically the same as the glm() reported on what is a presumably faster machine.

Cheers,
Marcus
